# Overview



**FINCHES** (**F**irst-principle **I**nteractions via **CHE**mical **S**pecificity) is a Python package for predicting intermolecular interactions driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Rather than relying on top-down empirical fitting, FINCHES starts from the bottom up: it uses physics-based coarse-grained forcefields to compute per-residue and per-fragment interaction energies directly from amino acid sequences, then aggregates those energies into quantitative predictions about binding specificity and phase behavior. The package was published in *Science* (2025) and is available as a standalone Python library, a set of Google Colab notebooks, and a webserver at [finches-online.com](https://www.finches-online.com/).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L30), [docs/index.rst](/docs/index.rst#L1-L48)

## What FINCHES Predicts

FINCHES answers four central questions about disordered region interactions. **First**, it generates **interaction maps** (intermaps) — 2D heatmaps where each pixel represents the predicted interaction strength between a sliding-window fragment of one sequence and a fragment of another, revealing which regions drive heterotypic or homotypic association. **Second**, it computes **per-residue interaction vectors** that decompose the overall interaction into attractive and repulsive contributions at each position, making it possible to pinpoint "sticky" residues. **Third**, it calculates a single **mean-field epsilon (ε) value** that quantifies the net interaction strength between two sequences — this scalar is the key input for higher-level thermodynamic reasoning. **Fourth**, it bridges that epsilon into **Flory-Huggins phase diagrams**, predicting whether a sequence will undergo liquid-liquid phase separation and how the phase boundary shifts with conditions like salt or pH. All four analyses share the same underlying forcefield engine, so results are internally consistent across scales.

Sources: [docs/index.rst](/docs/index.rst#L14-L40), [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L1-L50)

## Architecture at a Glance

The codebase is organized around a clean separation between **physics models** (forcefields), **computation engines** (epsilon and matrix constructors), and **user-facing interfaces** (frontends). This three-layer architecture means you can swap forcefields without changing analysis code, or access the same computation at different levels of abstraction depending on your needs.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Frontend Layer
        MF[Mpipi_frontend]
        CF[CALVADOS_frontend]
        FB[FinchesFrontend<br/>base class]
    end

    subgraph Computation Layer
        IMC[InteractionMatrixConstructor]
        ES[epsilon_stateless<br/>functions]
        ETF[epsilon_to_FHtheory]
        IV[interaction_vector]
    end

    subgraph Forcefield Layer
        MP[Mpipi_model<br/>Mpipi_original / Mpipi_GGv1]
        CM[calvados_model<br/>CALVADOS1 / CALVADOS2]
        CU[custom_model<br/>user-defined]
    end

    subgraph Analytical Layer
        FH[Flory-Huggins<br/>binodal / spinodal]
    end

    subgraph Supporting Tools
        PDB[PDB_structure_tools]
        DD[domain_decomposition]
        FDU[folded_domain_utils]
    end

    MF --> FB
    CF --> FB
    FB --> IMC
    MF --> MP
    CF --> CM
    IMC --> ES
    IMC --> MP
    IMC --> CM
    IMC --> CU
    ETF --> FH
    ETF --> ES
    IV --> IMC
    IV --> PDB
    PDB --> FDU
    DD --> FB
```

**Frontend Layer** — The `Mpipi_frontend` and `CALVADOS_frontend` classes inherit from a shared `FinchesFrontend` base. They bundle a forcefield model with an `InteractionMatrixConstructor`, exposing high-level methods like `epsilon()`, `interaction_figure()`, and `intermolecular_idr_matrix()` through a single object. Most users should start here.

**Computation Layer** — The `InteractionMatrixConstructor` is the engine that converts a forcefield into actionable calculations. It builds a pairwise lookup table from the model's `compute_interaction_parameter()` function, then provides methods for whole-sequence epsilon, sliding-window matrices, and weighted pairwise interactions. Stateless helper functions in `epsilon_stateless` handle matrix decomposition (attractive vs. repulsive) and vector construction without maintaining state.

**Forcefield Layer** — Each forcefield class encapsulates the physics: `Mpipi_model` loads the Mpipi-GG parameters (σ, ε, ν, μ, charge dictionaries) and computes the modified-Mpipi interaction potential; `calvados_model` builds Ashbaugh-Hatch + Yukawa potentials from CALVADOS2 stickiness parameters; `custom_model` lets you define arbitrary pairwise dictionaries with optional condition-dependent tuning. All three expose the same interface (`ALL_RESIDUES_TYPES`, `compute_interaction_parameter()`, `CONFIGS`), so the `InteractionMatrixConstructor` treats them uniformly.

Sources: [finches/__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L1-L24), [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L14-L50), [finches/epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L17-L100), [finches/forcefields/mpipi.py](/finches/forcefields/mpipi.py#L1-L40), [finches/forcefields/calvados.py](/finches/forcefields/calvados.py#L1-L50)

## Project Structure

```
finches/
├── __init__.py                    # Package entry: exports Mpipi_frontend, CALVADOS_frontend
├── frontend/
│   ├── frontend_base.py           # FinchesFrontend base class (shared logic)
│   ├── mpipi_frontend.py          # Mpipi_frontend (protein + RNA support)
│   ├── calvados_frontend.py       # CALVADOS_frontend (protein only, RNA guard)
│   └── interlogo.py               # Interaction logo generation
├── epsilon_calculation.py         # InteractionMatrixConstructor (core engine)
├── epsilon_stateless.py           # Pure functions: matrix ops, epsilon vectors
├── epsilon_to_FHtheory.py         # Bridge from epsilon → Flory-Huggins phase diagrams
├── interaction_vector.py          # Per-residue interaction vector plots
├── forcefields/
│   ├── mpipi.py                   # Mpipi_model (Mpipi_original, Mpipi_GGv1)
│   ├── calvados.py                # calvados_model (CALVADOS1, CALVADOS2)
│   ├── custom_model.py            # custom_model (user-defined pairwise)
│   └── calibration/               # Forcefield calibration scripts
├── analytical_fh/
│   ├── floryhuggins.py            # Binodal/spinodal wrapper
│   └── backend.py                 # Analytical FH solver (Qian et al. 2022)
├── PDB_structure_tools.py         # PDB → surface-accessible residue extraction
├── domain_decomposition/          # Identify interacting regions from intermaps
├── data/                          # Precomputed forcefield parameters (pickle)
├── utils/
│   ├── folded_domain_utils.py     # FoldedDomain class (SASA, surface masking)
│   └── matrix_manipulation.pyx    # Cython-accelerated matrix computation
└── tests/                         # pytest suite
```

Sources: [finches/__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L1-L24), [finches/epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L17-L50), [finches/forcefields/custom_model.py](/finches/forcefields/custom_model.py#L1-L30)

## Forcefield Comparison

FINCHES ships with two validated forcefields. Choosing between them determines the underlying physics, the supported residue types, and the condition-dependent parameters available.

| Feature | **Mpipi-GG** (`Mpipi_frontend`) | **CALVADOS2** (`CALVADOS_frontend`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Underlying potential** | Modified Mpipi (σ, ε, ν, μ + charge) | Ashbaugh-Hatch LJ + Yukawa DH |
| **Source publication** | Joseph et al. 2021; Lotthammer et al. 2024 | Tesei et al. 2021 |
| **Protein support** | 20 standard amino acids | 20 standard amino acids |
| **RNA support** | Yes (residue `U`) | No (raises `ValueError` on `U`) |
| **Tunable conditions** | `salt`, `dielectric` | `salt`, `pH`, `temp` |
| **Default charge_prefactor** | 0.20 | 0.70 |
| **Default null_interaction_baseline** | −0.128533 | −0.45 |
| **Recommended for** | Protein–protein and protein–RNA IDRs | Protein-only IDRs with pH/temperature studies |

> [!TIP]
> The `null_interaction_baseline` is the threshold that separates attractive from repulsive pairwise interactions. It is calibrated per-forcefield to reproduce the behavior of a poly(GS) reference sequence (expected to act as a non-interacting Gaussian chain). This means you **cannot** compare raw epsilon values across forcefields — only the ranking of sequences within a single forcefield is meaningful.

Sources: [finches/forcefields/mpipi.py](/finches/forcefields/mpipi.py#L17-L35), [finches/forcefields/calvados.py](/finches/forcefields/calvados.py#L26-L50), [finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L18-L28)

## Quick Usage Example

The simplest way to use FINCHES is through the frontend objects. After installation, import a frontend, instantiate it, and pass amino acid sequences as strings:

```python
from finches import Mpipi_frontend, CALVADOS_frontend

# Instantiate frontends with default conditions
mf = Mpipi_frontend()          # salt=0.150, dielectric=80.0
cf = CALVADOS_frontend()       # salt=0.150, pH=7.4, temp=288

# Define a sequence (DDX4 N-terminal domain)
ddx4_ntd = 'MGDEDWEAEINPHMSSYVPIFEKDRYSGENGDNFNRTPASSSEMDDGPSRRDHFMKSGFASGRNFGNRDAGECNKRDNTSTMGGFGVGKSFGNRGFSNSRFEDGDSSGFWRESSNDCEDNPTRNRGFSKRGGYRDGNNSEASGPYRRGGRGSFRGCRGGFGLGSPNNDLDPDECMQRTGGLFGSRRPVLSGTGNGDTSQSRSGSGSERGGYKGLNEEVITGSGKNSWKSEAEGGES'

# Compute homotypic epsilon (scalar interaction strength)
print(mf.epsilon(ddx4_ntd, ddx4_ntd))

# Generate an interaction map figure
mf.interaction_figure(ddx4_ntd, ddx4_ntd)

# Compute the sliding-window interaction matrix
matrix, disorder1, disorder2 = mf.intermolecular_idr_matrix(ddx4_ntd, ddx4_ntd)
```

The `epsilon()` method returns a single float summarizing the net interaction; `interaction_figure()` produces a matplotlib heatmap with parallel disorder tracks; `intermolecular_idr_matrix()` returns the raw matrix and per-sequence disorder profiles for custom analysis.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L40-L75), [finches/__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L20-L24), [finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L11-L30)

## Three Interfaces, One Goal

FINCHES is accessible through three complementary interfaces, each suited to a different workflow:

| Interface | Best for | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Python package** | Programmatic analysis, batch computation, integration into pipelines | `pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git` |
| **Google Colab** | Zero-install exploration, teaching, one-off analyses | [finches-colab](https://github.com/idptools/finches-colab) |
| **Webserver** | Quick lookups without any setup, sharing results with non-coders | [finches-online.com](https://www.finches-online.com/) |

The Python package offers full control over every parameter (window size, weighting schemes, null shuffles, custom forcefields). The Colab notebooks provide guided walkthroughs. The webserver exposes the most common operations through a browser UI.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L8-L15)

## Key Concepts to Understand

Before diving into the detailed documentation, four conceptual pillars underpin every FINCHES computation:

**Epsilon (ε)** is the mean-field interaction parameter. It is computed by building a pairwise interaction matrix between two sequences, separating attractive from repulsive contributions using the `null_interaction_baseline`, applying optional charge and aliphatic weighting schemes, and averaging. A more negative ε indicates stronger net attraction. This is the fundamental quantity from which all other predictions derive.

**Interaction maps** are computed via a sliding-window approach: each sequence is decomposed into overlapping fragments of a configurable window size (default 31 residues), and the epsilon is computed for every pair of fragments. The resulting 2D matrix reveals spatially resolved interaction patterns — for example, a specific charged patch on one IDR driving association with an aromatic patch on another.

**Weighting schemes** refine the raw pairwise matrix. *Charge weighting* reduces the repulsive contribution of like-charge pairs, reflecting the fact that charged sidechains can reorient away from each other in a disordered chain. *Aliphatic weighting* boosts the contribution of aliphatic residues that are surrounded by other aliphatic residues, capturing the cooperative effect of hydrophobic patches. Both are enabled by default and are controlled by the `charge_prefactor` parameter specific to each forcefield.

**Phase diagrams** connect epsilon to macroscopic behavior via Flory-Huggins theory. The epsilon value maps to the Flory-Huggins χ parameter, and the analytical binodal/spinodal curves from Qian et al. (2022) predict the coexistence concentrations. This bridge enables sequence-level mutations to be directly linked to shifts in phase boundaries.

> [!TIP]
> FINCHES predictions are most reliable for **comparative** analyses — e.g., "does mutation X increase or decrease phase separation propensity relative to the wildtype?" — rather than absolute quantitative predictions of critical concentrations. The mean-field framework necessarily simplifies chain connectivity, solvation, and many-body effects. The documentation's caveats sections discuss these limitations in detail.

Sources: [finches/epsilon_stateless.py](/finches/epsilon_stateless.py#L85-L160), [finches/epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L17-L100), [finches/analytical_fh/floryhuggins.py](/finches/analytical_fh/floryhuggins.py#L1-L60), [finches/epsilon_to_FHtheory.py](/finches/epsilon_to_FHtheory.py#L1-L30)

# Quick Start



Get from zero to your first interaction prediction in under five minutes. This guide walks you through installing FINCHES, initializing a frontend object, and computing your first **epsilon** interaction value — the core metric that quantifies the chemical specificity between two intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).

## Prerequisites

FINCHES requires **Python 3.9+** (3.11 or 3.12 recommended for performance) and depends on `numpy`, `scipy`, `cython`, `pytorch`, `mdtraj`, and `metapredict`. The table below summarizes the supported installation paths:

| Method | Best For | Command |
|--------|----------|---------|
| pip from GitHub | Most users | `pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git` |
| Local editable install | Contributors / developers | `git clone git@github.com:idptools/finches.git` → `cd finches` → `pip install -e .` |
| Google Colab | Zero-install exploration | [finches-colab notebooks](https://github.com/idptools/finches-colab) |
| Web server | Quick lookups, no code | [finches-online.com](https://www.finches-online.com/) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L75-L155), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L13-L31)

## Installation

### Step 1 — Create and activate a conda environment

```bash
conda create -n finches python=3.12 -y
conda activate finches
```

### Step 2 — Install core dependencies via conda

This ensures consistent NumPy/PyTorch builds (critical on macOS where mixing conda and PyPI builds causes failures):

```bash
conda install numpy pytorch scipy cython matplotlib jupyter -c pytorch
conda install mdtraj
pip install metapredict
```

### Step 3 — Install FINCHES

```bash
pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git
```

### Step 4 — Verify the installation

```bash
python -c "from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import Mpipi_frontend; mf = Mpipi_frontend(); print('Success')"
```

> **Note:** The first import takes 60–90 seconds while Cython-compiled modules are loaded. Subsequent imports are fast.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L83-L158), [docs/getting_started.rst](/docs/getting_started.rst#L22-L40)

## Your First Calculation

The diagram below shows the minimal workflow from sequence to prediction. FINCHES follows a **frontend pattern**: you instantiate a forcefield-specific frontend object, then call its methods with amino acid sequences.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Import frontend"] --> B["Instantiate object<br/>(choose forcefield)"]
    B --> C["Define sequence(s)<br/>as Python strings"]
    C --> D["Call .epsilon()"]
    D --> E["Get interaction value<br/>(float)"]
    style A fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
    style B fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
    style C fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00
    style D fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#7b1fa2
    style E fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c62828
```

### Initialize a frontend

FINCHES exposes two frontend classes — **`Mpipi_frontend`** and **`CALVADOS_frontend`** — that provide identical interfaces backed by different forcefield parameterizations:

```python
from finches import Mpipi_frontend, CALVADOS_frontend

# Mpipi-GG forcefield (supports protein AND RNA via 'U' residues)
mf = Mpipi_frontend(salt=0.150, dielectric=80.0)

# CALVADOS2 forcefield (protein only; pH- and temperature-sensitive)
cf = CALVADOS_frontend(salt=0.150, pH=7.4, temp=288)
```

Both constructors default to roughly physiological conditions. The key difference: `Mpipi_frontend` accepts `salt` and `dielectric`, while `CALVADOS_frontend` accepts `salt`, `pH`, and `temp` (in Kelvin).

Sources: [finches/__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L16-L17), [finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L12-L21), [finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L34-L43)

### Compute an epsilon value

The **epsilon** value is a scalar proxy for the interaction free energy between two IDR sequences — more negative means more attractive, more positive means more repulsive, and zero corresponds to a neutral GS-linker reference:

```python
# DDX4 N-terminal domain (a well-studied phase-separating IDR)
ddx4_ntd = 'MGDEDWEAEINPHMSSYVPIFEKDRYSGENGDNFNRTPASSSEMDDGPSRRDHFMKSGFASGRNFGNRDAGECNKRDNTSTMGGFGVGKSFGNRGFSNSRFEDGDSSGFWRESSNDCEDNPTRNRGFSKRGGYRDGNNSEASGPYRRGGRGSFRGCRGGFGLGSPNNDLDPDECMQRTGGLFGSRRPVLSGTGNGDTSQSRSGSGSERGGYKGLNEEVITGSGKNSWKSEAEGGES'

# Homotypic interaction (DDX4 with itself)
print(mf.epsilon(ddx4_ntd, ddx4_ntd))
```

For **heterotypic** interactions, simply pass two different sequences:

```python
seq_A = 'GGGGGRRRRR'   # a short arginine-rich motif
seq_B = 'GGGGGYYYYY'   # a short tyrosine-rich motif

print(mf.epsilon(seq_A, seq_B))  # attractive if π–cation contacts dominate
```

> [!TIP]
> The epsilon value is **order-dependent** (extrinsic): `epsilon(A, B) ≠ epsilon(B, A)` in general. Think of the first sequence as "bathed in" the second. To recover an intrinsic (order-independent) value, divide by the length of the first sequence: `epsilon(A, B) / len(A) == epsilon(B, A) / len(B)`.

Sources: [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L206-L241), [README.md](/README.md#L36-L43), [demo/overview_uses/basic_uses.ipynb](/demo/overview_uses/basic_uses.ipynb#L140-L175)

### Generate an interaction map

Beyond a single scalar, the **interaction figure** produces a 2D heatmap showing position-resolved interaction strength across both sequences — ideal for identifying which subregions drive binding:

```python
mf.interaction_figure(ddx4_ntd, ddx4_ntd)
```

This computes a sliding-window interaction matrix and renders it with parallel disorder prediction tracks. The returned tuple contains the matplotlib figure and axes objects for further customization.

Sources: [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L288-L416), [finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L128-L149)

## Core Frontend API at a Glance

Both `Mpipi_frontend` and `CALVADOS_frontend` expose the same set of high-level methods. The table below summarizes the primary entry points you'll use most often:

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `epsilon(seq1, seq2)` | `float` | Scalar interaction energy between two full sequences |
| `epsilon_vectors(seq1, seq2)` | tuple of arrays | Per-residue attractive and repulsive interaction vectors |
| `intermolecular_idr_matrix(seq1, seq2)` | `(matrix_tuple, disorder_1, disorder_2)` | Raw sliding-window interaction matrix + disorder profiles |
| `interaction_figure(seq1, seq2)` | `(fig, im, ax_main, ...)` | Rendered 2D interaction heatmap with disorder tracks |
| `per_residue_attractive_vector(seq1, seq2)` | `(indices, values)` | Per-residue average of attractive interactions (identifies "stickers") |
| `per_residue_repulsive_vector(seq1, seq2)` | `(indices, values)` | Per-residue average of repulsive interactions (identifies "spacers") |

All methods accept `use_aliphatic_weighting` and `use_charge_weighting` flags (default `True`) that apply correction terms for hydrophobic and charge-context effects.

Sources: [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L206-L282), [finches/frontend/frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L570-L696)

## Choosing a Forcefield

| Feature | `Mpipi_frontend` | `CALVADOS_frontend` |
|---------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Underlying model | Mpipi-GG v1 | CALVADOS2 |
| Constructor params | `salt`, `dielectric` | `salt`, `pH`, `temp` |
| RNA support (`U` residue) | ✅ Yes | ❌ No (raises `ValueError`) |
| Best for | Protein–protein and protein–RNA | Protein–protein with pH/temperature sensitivity |
| Primary citation | Joseph et al. (2021) + Lotthammer et al. (2024) | Tesei et al. (2022) |

For most protein-only use cases, either forcefield works well. Use `Mpipi_frontend` when working with RNA-containing sequences (use `U` for uracil); use `CALVADOS_frontend` when you need pH- or temperature-dependent predictions.

Sources: [finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L12-L21), [finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L16-L25), [finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L28-L43)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'finches'` | FINCHES not installed | Run `pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git` |
| First import takes >60s | Cython compilation on first load | Normal — subsequent imports are fast |
| `ValueError: CALVADOS2 cannot handle RNA ('U')` | `U` residue in CALVADOS input | Switch to `Mpipi_frontend` which supports RNA |
| `ImportError` for `metapredict` | Missing pip-only dependency | Run `pip install metapredict` |
| macOS NumPy/PyTorch crash | Mixed conda + PyPI builds | Install both via conda: `conda install numpy pytorch -c pytorch` |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L94-L109), [finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L16-L25)

# Installation Guide



This guide walks you through every step needed to get **FINCHES** (First-principle Interactions via CHEmical Specificity) installed and verified on your system. FINCHES is a Python package for computing IDR-associated chemical specificity, and its installation involves a compiled Cython extension alongside several scientific Python dependencies. By the end of this page, you will have a working environment ready for [Quick Start](2-quick-start) exploration.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L176), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L76)

## Prerequisites

Before installing FINCHES, review the following requirements and constraints to ensure a smooth setup:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Python version** | ≥ 3.7 required; **3.11 or 3.12 recommended** for best performance |
| **License** | CC BY-NC 4.0 — **non-commercial use only** |
| **C++ compiler** | Required for Cython extension compilation (bundled with most OS dev tools) |
| **Git** | Required for both installation methods |
| **Conda** (recommended) | For managing the environment and dependency ecosystem |

> [!TIP]
> FINCHES includes a Cython-compiled module (`matrix_manipulation.pyx`) that accelerates matrix operations. This extension is built during installation and requires a working C compiler. On macOS, ensure Xcode Command Line Tools are installed (`xcode-select --install`). On Linux, `gcc` is typically available by default.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L26-L31), [setup.py](/setup.py#L1-L30), [LICENSE](/LICENSE#L1-L5)

## Core Dependencies

FINCHES depends on the following runtime packages, declared in `pyproject.toml`. Understanding these helps troubleshoot any version conflicts:

| Package | Version Constraint | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `numpy` | (≥ 2 recommended) | Array operations, Cython include paths |
| `afrc` | ≥ 0.3.4 | Analytical FRC (Flory Random Coil) scaling |
| `scipy` | any | Numerical integration and optimization |
| `soursop` | ≥ 0.2.4 | Polymer physics calculations |
| `pandas` | any | Data structure manipulation |
| `metapredict` | any (pip-only) | Intrinsically disordered region prediction |
| `ipython` | any | Interactive computing support |

The **build-time** dependencies (needed only during installation) are `setuptools≥61.0`, `wheel`, `versioningit≈2.0`, `cython`, and `numpy`.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L29-L31), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L8)

## Installation Methods at a Glance

The following flowchart illustrates the two supported installation paths and their decision criteria:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start: Create & activate conda env"] --> B["Install conda ecosystem deps"]
    B --> C{"Plan to modify<br/>FINCHES source code?"}
    C -->|"No — just use it"| D["Method 1: pip install from GitHub"]
    C -->|"Yes — develop/contribute"| E["Method 2: Clone + editable install"]
    D --> F["Verify installation"]
    E --> F
    F --> G{{"✅ FINCHES ready"}}

    style A fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7d2d
    style G fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7d2d
    style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404
```

### Method 1: Direct pip Install from GitHub

This is the **recommended approach** for most users. It installs a frozen copy of FINCHES directly into your active environment without cloning the repository locally.

```bash
pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git
```

This command fetches the latest `main` branch, compiles the Cython extension, and installs all dependencies automatically. It can be run from any directory — the package lands in your environment's site-packages.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L113-L118)

### Method 2: Clone and Editable Install

Use this method if you intend to modify the source code, contribute fixes, or want the convenience of updating via `git pull`. **Clone to a sensible working directory** — the repository will be copied to that location.

```bash
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone git@github.com:idptools/finches.git

# 2. Enter the project root (where pyproject.toml lives)
cd finches

# 3. Install in editable mode
pip install -e .
```

The `-e` (editable) flag creates a live link to the source directory rather than copying files into site-packages. This provides two critical advantages:

1. **Instant updates** — running `git pull` inside the cloned directory immediately reflects code changes the next time you import FINCHES, with no reinstallation required.
2. **Correct Cython compilation** — the Cython extension (`matrix_manipulation.pyx`) is compiled in-place during an editable install. A non-editable pip install currently has a known packaging issue where the compiled `.so` file may not be correctly distributed.

> [!TIP]
> If you use Method 2 and later switch to a different branch or pull major changes, the Cython `.so` file won't automatically recompile. Re-run `pip install -e .` to rebuild the extension after significant updates.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L120-L145), [setup.py](/setup.py#L17-L29)

## Step-by-Step: Conda Environment Setup

The following procedure has been tested in a clean conda environment and represents the most reliable installation path. It carefully manages the dependency ecosystem to avoid the cross-platform numpy conflicts that can occur when mixing conda and PyPI packages.

### Step 1 — Create and Activate the Environment

```bash
conda create -n finches python=3.12 -y
conda activate finches
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L84-L91)

### Step 2 — Install Ecosystem Dependencies via Conda

Install the core scientific packages **from conda** to ensure ABI compatibility. This is especially important on macOS where mixing conda and PyPI numpy/PyTorch builds causes segfaults.

```bash
# Install from the pytorch channel for consistent ABI
conda install numpy pytorch scipy cython matplotlib jupyter -c pytorch

# mdtraj is installed separately (different channel/dependency chain)
conda install mdtraj
```

### Step 3 — Install pip-Only Dependencies

```bash
# metapredict is only distributed via PyPI
pip install metapredict
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L94-L108)

### Step 4 — Install FINCHES

Choose Method 1 or Method 2 from the sections above. For most users:

```bash
pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L110-L118)

### Step 5 — Verify the Installation

Navigate away from the install directory (to avoid import confusion) and run the verification command:

```bash
cd ~
python -c "from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import Mpipi_frontend; mf = Mpipi_frontend(); print('Success')"
```

If the output is `Success`, FINCHES is correctly installed and the forcefield data and Cython extension are accessible. The first invocation may take a moment as Python compiles and caches imported modules.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L147-L158)

## Complete Installation Summary

The table below provides a single-copy reference for the full installation sequence from a fresh system:

| Step | Command | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `conda create -n finches python=3.12 -y` | Create isolated environment |
| 2 | `conda activate finches` | Activate the environment |
| 3 | `conda install numpy pytorch scipy cython matplotlib jupyter -c pytorch` | Core scientific deps (conda) |
| 4 | `conda install mdtraj` | Trajectory analysis dep (conda) |
| 5 | `pip install metapredict` | IDR prediction dep (PyPI only) |
| 6a | `pip install git+https://git@github.com/idptools/finches.git` | Install FINCHES (direct) |
| 6b | `git clone git@github.com:idptools/finches.git && cd finches && pip install -e .` | Install FINCHES (editable) |
| 7 | `python -c "from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import Mpipi_frontend; mf = Mpipi_frontend(); print('Success')"` | Verify installation |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L75-L158), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L29-L31)

## Platform-Specific Notes

### macOS

On Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) and Intel Macs alike, the **most critical rule** is to install `numpy` and `pytorch` from the **same package ecosystem** — either both from conda or both from PyPI. Mixing them produces segmentation faults due to incompatible C ABI bindings. The conda-first approach in the step-by-step guide above avoids this by design.

Ensure Xcode Command Line Tools are installed before running `pip install`, as the Cython extension requires a C compiler:

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

### Linux

Linux systems typically ship with `gcc` pre-installed. If not, install it via your distribution's package manager (`sudo apt install build-essential` on Debian/Ubuntu). No other platform-specific steps are needed.

### Windows

FINCHES has not been officially tested on Windows. The recommended path for Windows users is to use **Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)** with a conda distribution installed inside the WSL environment, then follow the Linux instructions.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L76-L78), [setup.py](/setup.py#L1-L30)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'finches.utils.matrix_manipulation'` | Cython `.pyx` not compiled to `.so` | Re-run `pip install -e .` from the project root, or use Method 1 instead |
| `ImportError: numpy.core.multiarray failed to import` | numpy version mismatch between compile-time and runtime | Reinstall numpy in the active env: `conda install numpy --force-reinstall` |
| Segmentation fault on import | Mixed conda/PyPI numpy + pytorch | Remove and reinstall both from conda: `conda install numpy pytorch -c pytorch` |
| `versioningit` errors during install | Missing build dependency | Install separately: `pip install versioningit` then retry |
| `metapredict` not found | Not installed via pip | `pip install metapredict` (conda does not distribute this package) |
| Slow first import | Normal — Python caches bytecode on first run | Subsequent imports will be fast; no action needed |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L76-L158), [setup.py](/setup.py#L17-L29), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L8)

## What Gets Installed

Understanding the package layout helps diagnose import issues and know where data files reside. The following diagram shows the installed package structure at a glance:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph finches["finches/"]
        A["__init__.py<br/>(exports frontends)"]
        B["frontend/<br/>(Mpipi, CALVADOS)"]
        C["forcefields/<br/>(models + data)"]
        D["epsilon_calculation.py"]
        E["utils/matrix_manipulation<br/>(Cython .pyx → .so)"]
        F["data/<br/>(forcefield .pickle)"]
        G["analytical_fh/<br/>(Flory-Huggins)"]
        H["domain_decomposition/"]

    style E fill:#ffe0e0,stroke:#cc3333
    style F fill:#e0e0ff,stroke:#3333cc
```

The **red** node (`matrix_manipulation`) is the Cython-compiled module — if this file is missing its compiled `.so` counterpart, FINCHES will fail on import. The **blue** node (`data/`) contains serialized forcefield parameter files (`.pickle`) that are loaded at runtime by the frontend objects.

Sources: [finches/__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L1-L24), [setup.py](/setup.py#L12-L22), [MANIFEST.in](/MANIFEST.in#L1-L17)
