# Architecture Overview



FINCHES (**F**irst-principle **I**nteractions via **CHE**mical **S**pecificity) is organized as a four-layer architecture that cleanly separates user interaction, core computation, biophysical models, and parameter data. This page maps the complete module topology, traces the primary data flow from amino acid sequences through to phase diagrams, and identifies the design patterns that make the system extensible across multiple forcefield models.

Sources: [__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L1-L24), [README.md](/README.md#L1-L176)

## Structural Layers

The codebase is partitioned into four distinct layers, each with a single responsibility. The **Frontend Layer** exposes the user-facing API and handles visualization. The **Core Computation Layer** implements the mathematical machinery for building interaction matrices, computing epsilon values, and constructing per-residue vectors. The **Forcefield Layer** encapsulates biophysical models as interchangeable plug-ins. The **Data Layer** stores precomputed parameter sets as pickled dictionaries. This separation ensures that adding a new forcefield never requires changes to the computation or frontend code.

```
finches/
├── frontend/                  ← Layer 1: User-facing API & Visualization
│   ├── frontend_base.py           FinchesFrontend (abstract base class)
│   ├── mpipi_frontend.py          Mpipi_frontend (concrete)
│   ├── calvados_frontend.py       CALVADOS_frontend (concrete)
│   └── interlogo.py               Logo generation utilities
│
├── epsilon_calculation.py    ← Layer 2: Core Computation
├── epsilon_stateless.py          Stateless vector/epsilon functions
├── epsilon_to_FHtheory.py        Bridge to Flory-Huggins theory
├── interaction_vector.py         Interaction vector plotting
├── sequence_tools.py             Sequence property calculators (FCR, NCPR)
├── parsing_aminoacid_sequences.py Sequence parsing utilities
│
├── forcefields/               ← Layer 3: Forcefield Models (Interface Pattern)
│   ├── mpipi.py                   Mpipi_model
│   ├── calvados.py                calvados_model
│   ├── custom_model.py            custom_model (user-defined)
│   └── calibration/              Calibration data & scripts
│
├── analytical_fh/            ← Layer 2b: Flory-Huggins Solver
│   ├── backend.py                 Original Qian et al. solver
│   └── floryhuggins.py            Wrapper API
│
├── domain_decomposition/     ← Cross-cutting: Region Analysis
│   └── domain_analysis.py         InteractingRegions, extract_regions
│
├── PDB_structure_tools.py    ← Cross-cutting: Folded Domain Integration
│
├── utils/                    ← Performance: Cython Acceleration
│   ├── matrix_manipulation.pyx    dict2matrix, matrix_scan (Cython)
│   └── folded_domain_utils.py     Folded domain helper functions
│
├── data/                     ← Layer 4: Parameter Data
│   ├── Mpipi/                     Mpipi pickled parameter files
│   ├── calvados/                  CALVADOS pickled parameter files
│   ├── fingerprints.py            Parameter fingerprinting
│   ├── forcefield_dependencies.py Baseline & prefactor computation
│   └── reference_sequence_info.py Reference sequence data
│
└── tests/                    ← Verification
    ├── test_epsilon_calculation.py
    ├── test_FH_diagrams.py
    ├── test_finches.py
    └── test_frontend_mpipi.py
```

Sources: [__init__.py](/finches/__init__.py#L1-L24), [epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L1-L50), [frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend_base.py#L1-L30)

## Core Design Patterns

FINCHES employs two primary design patterns that govern how modules interact.

### Interface Pattern: InteractionMatrixConstructor

The **InteractionMatrixConstructor** is the architectural linchpin. It accepts any forcefield object that implements a required contract — specifically `ALL_RESIDUES_TYPES`, `compute_interaction_parameter(r1, r2)`, and `CONFIGS` — and provides a uniform API for computing pairwise matrices, weighted matrices, epsilon values, and sliding-window matrices regardless of the underlying biophysical model. This is the classic Interface (or Strategy) pattern: the computation algorithm is fixed, while the interaction parameter source is interchangeable.

| Forcefield Contract Method | Purpose | Defined In |
|---|---|---|
| `ALL_RESIDUES_TYPES` | List of valid residue groups (e.g., protein + RNA) | All forcefield classes |
| `compute_interaction_parameter(r1, r2)` | Returns pairwise interaction value for residue pair | All forcefield classes |
| `CONFIGS` | Dictionary with `charge_prefactor` and `null_interaction_baseline` | All forcefield classes |

Sources: [epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L29-L100)

### Inheritance Pattern: FinchesFrontend Hierarchy

The **Frontend** layer uses class inheritance to share implementation while allowing model-specific customization. `FinchesFrontend` is an abstract base class that defines shared methods (`intermolecular_idr_matrix`, `epsilon`, `interaction_figure`, `per_residue_attractive_vector`). `Mpipi_frontend` and `CALVADOS_frontend` derive from it, each constructing their own forcefield model and `InteractionMatrixConstructor` instance, then delegating to the superclass for computation. The `CALVADOS_frontend` additionally applies an `@RNA_check` decorator to reject RNA-containing sequences, since CALVADOS2 does not support nucleic acid residues.

| Class | Parent | Forcefield | RNA Support | Key Override |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `FinchesFrontend` | — | None (abstract) | — | Cannot be instantiated directly |
| `Mpipi_frontend` | `FinchesFrontend` | `Mpipi_GGv1` | ✅ (via `U` residue) | Handles `U` → disables disorder prediction |
| `CALVADOS_frontend` | `FinchesFrontend` | `CALVADOS2` | ❌ | `@RNA_check` decorator on all methods |

Sources: [frontend_base.py](/finches/frontend_base.py#L12-L28), [mpipi_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L1-L15), [calvados_frontend.py](/finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L1-L40)

## Data Flow Architecture

The following diagram traces the primary computational pipeline from amino acid sequences to final outputs. Every analysis in FINCHES follows this core path, with optional branches for phase diagrams and folded domain interactions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SEQ["Amino Acid Sequences<br/>(seq1, seq2)"] --> PARSE["Sequence Validation<br/>& Conversion"]
    PARSE --> FF["Forcefield Model<br/>(Mpipi / CALVADOS / Custom)"]
    
    FF --> LOOKUP["Pairwise Lookup Table<br/>lookup[r1][r2] → value"]
    LOOKUP --> PWM["Pairwise Matrix<br/>(N×M numpy array)"]
    
    PWM --> CW["Context Weighting<br/>• Aliphatic weighting<br/>• Charge weighting"]
    CW --> WM["Weighted Matrix"]
    
    WM --> SPLIT["Attractive / Repulsive<br/>Split at null_interaction_baseline"]
    SPLIT --> EPS["ε Value<br/>(scalar interaction strength)"]
    SPLIT --> VEC["ε Vectors<br/>(per-residue attractive/repulsive)"]
    
    WM --> SW["Sliding Window Scan<br/>(Cython-accelerated)"]
    SW --> IM["Interaction Matrix<br/>(position-resolved ε map)"]
    
    EPS --> FH["Flory-Huggins<br/>Phase Diagram"]
    IM --> FIG["Interaction Figure<br/>(heatmap + disorder tracks)"]
    VEC --> VPL["Interaction Vector Plot"]
    
    PDB["PDB Structure"] --> SAFD["Surface-Accessible<br/>Folded Domain Residues"]
    SAFD --> IDV["Inter-domain ε Vectors"]
    
    style SEQ fill:#e1f5fe
    style FF fill:#fff3e0
    style EPS fill:#e8f5e9
    style IM fill:#e8f5e9
    style FH fill:#f3e5f5
```

**Stage 1 — Sequence Intake & Validation**: Input sequences are validated against `ALL_RESIDUES_TYPES` to ensure all residues belong to a single residue group. An optional `sequence_converter` function can transform sequences before validation (used for masking or custom residue mapping).

**Stage 2 — Forcefield Resolution**: The forcefield model's `compute_interaction_parameter(r1, r2)` is called for every residue pair to populate a lookup dictionary. This happens once during `InteractionMatrixConstructor` initialization and again if `_update_parameters()` is called.

**Stage 3 — Matrix Construction**: The pairwise interaction matrix is built by indexing the lookup table for each (residue_i, residue_j) pair. The Cython-accelerated `dict2matrix()` function handles this for performance-critical paths.

**Stage 4 — Context Weighting**: Two optional weighting schemes modify the raw matrix. **Aliphatic weighting** amplifies interactions for residues surrounded by other aliphatic residues, capturing hydrophobic patch effects. **Charge weighting** reduces repulsion between oppositely charged neighbors (scaled by `charge_prefactor`), modeling sidechain reorientation and pKa shifts.

**Stage 5 — Epsilon Computation**: The weighted matrix is split at the `null_interaction_baseline` (calibrated against poly(GS) sequences as a Gaussian chain reference) into attractive and repulsive components. Summing and averaging yields either a scalar ε value or per-residue ε vectors.

**Stage 6 — Sliding Window Scan**: For interaction maps, the sequences are decomposed into overlapping windows and ε is computed per window pair, producing a position-resolved 2D matrix. The Cython `matrix_scan()` function provides ~12× speedup over pure Python for this step.

Sources: [epsilon_calculation.py](/finches/epsilon_calculation.py#L200-L400), [epsilon_stateless.py](/finches/epsilon_stateless.py#L1-L200), [matrix_manipulation.pyx](/finches/utils/matrix_manipulation.pyx#L1-L80)

## Forcefield Model Comparison

The three forcefield models differ in their physical basis, parameter sources, and supported residue types. All three implement the same contract, making them interchangeable within `InteractionMatrixConstructor`.

| Property | Mpipi (Mpipi_GGv1) | CALVADOS (CALVADOS2) | Custom Model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Physical Basis** | Mie potential + Debye-Hückel | Ashbaugh-Hatch LJ + Yukawa | User-defined |
| **Parameter Source** | Joseph et al. 2021, Lotthammer et al. 2024 | Tesei et al. 2021 | User-provided dictionary |
| **Condition Dependence** | Salt, dielectric | Salt, pH, temperature | Arbitrary via callback |
| **RNA Support** | ✅ (U residue) | ❌ | User-defined |
| **Parameter Storage** | 5 pickled dicts (σ, ε, ν, μ, charge) | 1 pickled DataFrame | Inline dictionary |
| **Default charge_prefactor** | 0.20 | 0.70 | User-defined |
| **Default null_interaction_baseline** | −0.128533 | −0.45 | User-defined |

The `custom_model` class enables arbitrary forcefield definitions by accepting a flat dictionary of pairwise interactions (e.g., `{'A_A': -1, 'A_K': 0.5}`), an optional `condition_dictionary` for tunable parameters, and a `condition_dependence_function` callback that recalculates interactions when conditions change. This makes it possible to prototype novel coarse-grained models without modifying FINCHES source code.

Sources: [mpipi.py](/finches/forcefields/mpipi.py#L1-L50), [calvados.py](/finches/forcefields/calvados.py#L1-L80), [custom_model.py](/finches/forcefields/custom_model.py#L1-L60)

## Cross-Cutting Modules

Several modules span multiple layers and integrate with external tools:

**Folded Domain Integration** (`PDB_structure_tools.py`): Uses `soursop` to parse PDB structures, compute solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) with a 7Å probe radius, and extract surface-accessible folded domain (SAFD) residues. These residues are then fed into `get_interdomain_epsilon_vectors()` to compute how an IDR interacts with the surface of an adjacent folded domain, accounting for spatial proximity via distance-dependent weighting.

**Domain Decomposition** (`domain_decomposition/domain_analysis.py`): Identifies contiguous interacting regions within the 2D interaction matrix using peak-finding on per-row/column ε profiles. Returns `InteractingRegions` objects that encapsulate start/end positions, sequences, and rectangle coordinates for overlay on interaction maps.

**Flory-Huggins Bridge** (`epsilon_to_FHtheory.py`): Converts computed ε values into Flory-Huggins χ parameters and constructs phase diagrams. Supports condition-dependent scanning across salt, pH, and dielectric values by iteratively re-initializing the forcefield model and recomputing ε at each condition point.

**Sequence Utilities** (`sequence_tools.py`): Provides sequence-level property calculators including fraction of charged residues (FCR), net charge per residue (NCPR), and κ (kappa) parameter for charge patterning analysis.

Sources: [PDB_structure_tools.py](/finches/PDB_structure_tools.py#L1-L80), [domain_analysis.py](/finches/domain_decomposition/domain_analysis.py#L1-L100), [epsilon_to_FHtheory.py](/finches/epsilon_to_FHtheory.py#L1-L50), [sequence_tools.py](/finches/sequence_tools.py#L1-L80)

## Performance Architecture

FINCHES uses Cython for two performance-critical operations. The `dict2matrix()` function converts the Python lookup dictionary into a NumPy 2D array using typed C-level loops with `@cython.boundscheck(False)`. The `matrix_scan()` function implements the sliding-window ε computation with pre-allocated arrays and C-level arithmetic, providing approximately **12× speedup** over the equivalent pure-Python implementation. Both are compiled at install time via the `cython` dependency and are automatically used when `use_cython=True` (the default) is passed to frontend methods.

> [!TIP]
> Always keep `use_cython=True` (the default) for production runs. The Cython path is transparently invoked — no code changes are needed. Only set `use_cython=False` for debugging, as the pure-Python fallback is significantly slower for large sequences.

Sources: [matrix_manipulation.pyx](/finches/utils/matrix_manipulation.pyx#L1-L80)

## Recommended Reading Path

Now that you understand the architecture, the following progression builds from user-facing APIs inward to computational details:

1. **[Mpipi and CALVADOS Frontends](5-mpipi-and-calvados-frontends)** — Start here to learn the primary API entry points
2. **[InteractionMatrixConstructor](8-interactionmatrixconstructor)** — Understand the core interface that connects frontends to forcefields
3. **[Epsilon Calculation and Weighting](9-epsilon-calculation-and-weighting)** — Dive into how interaction strength is quantified
4. **[Mpipi Forcefield Parameters](11-mpipi-forcefield-parameters)** — Examine the default forcefield model in detail
5. **[Flory-Huggins Phase Diagrams](14-flory-huggins-phase-diagrams)** — See how ε values predict phase behavior

# Mpipi and CALVADOS Frontends



The **Mpipi** and **CALVADOS** frontends are the primary user-facing interfaces in finches. They provide a unified, high-level API for computing intermolecular interaction energies, generating per-residue interaction vectors, building interaction matrix figures, and constructing Flory-Huggins phase diagrams — all without requiring direct interaction with the underlying forcefield parameters or computation engine. Each frontend wraps a specific coarse-grained forcefield model and delegates heavy computation to the shared `InteractionMatrixConstructor`, while adding model-specific validation, default parameters, and RNA handling logic.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L1-L30), [mpipi_frontend.py](finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L1-L25), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L1-L35)

## Architecture: Inheritance-Driven Design

Both frontends inherit from the abstract base class `FinchesFrontend`, which implements the full computational and visualization API. The derived classes override only their constructors (to bind the correct forcefield model) and a small number of methods that require model-specific input validation — most notably RNA sequence handling. This means every new method added to the base class automatically becomes available in both frontends, ensuring API consistency across models.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class FinchesFrontend {
        <<abstract>>
        +IMC_object : InteractionMatrixConstructor
        +intermolecular_idr_matrix(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +epsilon(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +epsilon_vectors(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +interaction_figure(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +per_residue_attractive_vector(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +per_residue_repulsive_vector(seq1, seq2, ...)
        +protein_nucleic_vector(seq, ...)
        +plot_protein_nucleic_vector(seq, ...)
        +build_phase_diagram(seq, ...)
        +plot_phase_diagram(seq, ...)
        +plot_multiple_phase_diagrams(seq_dict, ...)
    }

    class Mpipi_frontend {
        +model : Mpipi_model
        +__init__(salt, dielectric)
        +intermolecular_idr_matrix()$
        +interaction_figure()$
    }

    class CALVADOS_frontend {
        +model : calvados_model
        +__init__(salt, pH, temp)
        +intermolecular_idr_matrix()$
        +epsilon()$
        +interaction_figure()$
    }

    FinchesFrontend <|-- Mpipi_frontend
    FinchesFrontend <|-- CALVADOS_frontend

    note for Mpipi_frontend "$ = override with RNA-tolerant logic"
    note for CALVADOS_frontend "$ = override with RNA-check decorator"
```

The base class explicitly prevents direct instantiation — calling `FinchesFrontend()` raises a `TypeError`, forcing users to work through one of the concrete derived classes.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L25-L37)

## Instantiation and Constructor Parameters

Each frontend's constructor initializes two critical objects: the **forcefield model** (which encodes all residue-residue interaction parameters) and the **`InteractionMatrixConstructor`** (which uses that model for computation). The constructors differ in which physical conditions they expose:

| Frontend | Constructor Signature | Forcefield Model | Physical Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Mpipi_frontend` | `Mpipi_frontend(salt=0.150, dielectric=80.0)` | `Mpipi_model("Mpipi_GGv1")` | Salt concentration (M), Dielectric constant |
| `CALVADOS_frontend` | `CALVADOS_frontend(salt=0.150, pH=7.4, temp=288)` | `calvados_model("CALVADOS2")` | Salt concentration (M), pH, Temperature (K) |

**Key difference**: Mpipi exposes a `dielectric` parameter (screening via dielectric constant), while CALVADOS exposes `pH` and `temp` parameters (Henderson-Hasselbalch protonation and temperature-dependent electrostatics). Both default to **150 mM salt**, reflecting physiological ionic strength.

```python
# Mpipi frontend — dielectric-based electrostatics
from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import Mpipi_frontend
mf = Mpipi_frontend(salt=0.150, dielectric=80.0)

# CALVADOS frontend — pH and temperature-based electrostatics
from finches.frontend.calvados_frontend import CALVADOS_frontend
cf = CALVADOS_frontend(salt=0.150, pH=7.4, temp=288)
```

Sources: [mpipi_frontend.py](finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L9-L16), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L31-L41)

## Core API Methods

The following methods are available on **both** frontend objects. The table summarizes each method's purpose and return type:

| Method | Purpose | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `epsilon(seq1, seq2)` | Whole-sequence pairwise interaction energy | `float` |
| `epsilon_vectors(seq1, seq2)` | Attractive and repulsive epsilon decomposition vectors | `tuple` of arrays |
| `intermolecular_idr_matrix(seq1, seq2)` | Sliding-window interaction matrix with disorder profiles | `(matrix_tuple, disorder_1, disorder_2)` |
| `interaction_figure(seq1, seq2)` | Full visualization: heatmap + disorder tracks | `(fig, im, ax_main, ax_top, ax_right, ax_colorbar)` |
| `per_residue_attractive_vector(seq1, seq2)` | Per-residue average of attractive interactions | `(indices, values)` |
| `per_residue_repulsive_vector(seq1, seq2)` | Per-residue average of repulsive interactions | `(indices, values)` |
| `protein_nucleic_vector(seq)` | Per-residue protein–RNA binding profile (poly-U) | `(indices, values)` |
| `plot_protein_nucleic_vector(seq)` | Visualization of protein–RNA binding profile | `(fig, ax)` |
| `build_phase_diagram(seq)` | Flory-Huggins binodal + spinodal curves | 8-element tuple |
| `plot_phase_diagram(seq)` | Single-sequence phase diagram plot | `(phase_data, fig, ax)` |
| `plot_multiple_phase_diagrams(seq_dict)` | Overlay multiple phase diagrams | `(phase_data_list, fig, ax)` |

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L39-L1345)

### Epsilon: Whole-Sequence Interaction Energy

The simplest entry point computes a single scalar epsilon value for two full sequences. This delegates directly to `InteractionMatrixConstructor.calculate_epsilon_value()`:

```python
mf = Mpipi_frontend()
eps = mf.epsilon("MDVFKPGDKIIYTVKQEE", "KRTYADGEEYVQTVKPGK")
# Returns a float — negative = net attractive, positive = net repulsive
```

The `use_aliphatic_weighting` and `use_charge_weighting` flags (both default `True`) control whether local sequence context adjusts aliphatic and charge contributions, respectively.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L201-L232)

### Intermolecular IDR Matrix: Sliding-Window Computation

The `intermolecular_idr_matrix()` method is the computational backbone for region-resolved analysis. It decomposes both sequences into overlapping windows of `window_size` residues (default 31) and computes epsilon for every pair of windows, producing a 2D matrix where each cell represents the interaction energy between one region of `seq1` and one region of `seq2`.

The return value is a 3-tuple:

- **`[0]`** — The interaction matrix tuple itself: `(matrix_array, seq1_indices, seq2_indices)`. The `matrix_array` is a 2D NumPy array; the index arrays map matrix rows/columns back to sequence positions.
- **`[1]`** — Disorder profile for `seq1` (from metapredict), or all-1s array if `disorder_1=False`.
- **`[2]`** — Disorder profile for `seq2`, or all-1s array if `disorder_2=False`.

```python
mf = Mpipi_frontend()
result = mf.intermolecular_idr_matrix("MDVFKPGDKIIYTVKQEE", "KRTYADGEEYVQTVKPGK")
matrix_array = result[0][0]    # 2D sliding epsilon values
seq1_idx     = result[0][1]    # indices mapping rows to seq1 positions
seq2_idx     = result[0][2]    # indices mapping columns to seq2 positions
disorder_1   = result[1]       # disorder profile for seq1
disorder_2   = result[2]       # disorder profile for seq2
```

> [!TIP]
> The window edges are not padded, so the matrix dimensions are smaller than the sequence lengths by approximately `(window_size - 1)` on each side. Always use the returned index arrays to map matrix positions back to residue positions.

When `null_shuffle` is set to an integer (e.g., 100), the method generates that many sequence-shuffled null matrices, subtracts the mean null from the real matrix, and returns the shuffle-normalized result. For homotypic interactions (`seq1 == seq2`), the null is symmetrized to avoid artifacts.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L42-L197)

### Per-Residue Interaction Vectors

Two complementary methods decompose the interaction matrix into per-residue profiles along `seq1`:

- **`per_residue_attractive_vector()`** — For each residue in `seq1`, averages all **negative** (attractive) values across `seq2`. This identifies "sticker" regions without confounding from repulsive neighbors.
- **`per_residue_repulsive_vector()`** — For each residue in `seq1`, averages all **positive** (repulsive) values across `seq2`.

Both return `(indices, values)` and apply Savitzky-Golay smoothing by default (`smoothing_window=20`, `poly_order=3`). Set `smoothing_window=False` to disable smoothing. Set `return_total=True` to get the raw sum instead of the average.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L540-L795)

### Protein–Nucleic Acid Vector

The `protein_nucleic_vector()` method computes a per-residue profile of protein–RNA binding propensity by sliding a window across the protein sequence and computing epsilon against a poly-U RNA fragment of the same length. This is only available on frontends that support RNA (see the RNA handling section below). The result is smoothed with a Savitzky-Golay filter and returned as `(indices, values)`.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L800-L895)

### Interaction Figure

The `interaction_figure()` method produces a publication-quality composite figure containing: a central interaction matrix heatmap, parallel disorder profile bar plots along the top and right axes, and an integrated colorbar. When `zero_folded=True` (default), residues predicted as folded by metapredict are zeroed out in the matrix, reflecting the physical reality that folded domains are not available for IDR-like interactions.

The visualization parameters differ between frontends:

| Parameter | Mpipi Default | CALVADOS Default | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vmin` / `vmax` | -3 / 3 | -7.5 / 7.5 | CALVADOS epsilon values span a wider range |

Additional figure features include domain highlighting (`seq1_domains`, `seq2_domains`), position marker lines (`seq1_lines`, `seq2_lines`), and custom rectangle overlays (`plot_rectangles`).

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L236-L530), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L160-L175)

### Phase Diagrams

Three methods provide Flory-Huggins phase diagram computation and visualization:

1. **`build_phase_diagram(seq)`** — Computes the homotypic binodal and spinodal curves from the sequence's epsilon value. Returns an 8-element tuple with dilute/dense concentrations, critical points, and temperature arrays for both binodal and spinodal.
2. **`plot_phase_diagram(seq)`** — Plots a single sequence's binodal as temperature vs. volume fraction (φ).
3. **`plot_multiple_phase_diagrams(seq_dict)`** — Overlays multiple sequences' binodals. Accepts a dictionary of `{name: [sequence, color]}` and optionally normalizes temperatures by a reference sequence's critical temperature (`tc_ref`).

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L1020-L1345)

## RNA Sequence Handling: The Critical Difference

The most important functional distinction between the two frontends is how they handle RNA sequences (represented by the `U` residue code for uracil):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Sequence contains 'U'?"] --> B{Which frontend?}
    B -->|Mpipi| C["RNA tolerated as poly-U<br/>Disorder prediction disabled for U-containing seq"]
    B -->|CALVADOS| D["ValueError raised:<br/>CALVADOS2 cannot handle RNA ('U')"]
    C --> E["Compute normally"]
    D --> F["Exception propagates to caller"]
```

**Mpipi** accommodates RNA as poly-U fragments — the Mpipi forcefield includes parameters for uracil. When a sequence contains `U`, the frontend automatically disables disorder prediction for that sequence (since metapredict only handles protein sequences) but proceeds with computation.

**CALVADOS** explicitly **rejects** any sequence containing `U`. This is enforced through the `@RNA_check` decorator, which inspects `seq1` and `seq2` before any computation begins and raises a `ValueError` with the message `"CALVADOS2 cannot handle RNA ('U')"`. This decorator is applied to `intermolecular_idr_matrix()`, `epsilon()`, and `interaction_figure()` in the CALVADOS frontend.

Additionally, CALVADOS provides a stub `protein_nucleic_vector()` that unconditionally raises an exception, since protein–RNA computation is inherently unsupported.

> [!TIP]
> Always check your sequences for `U` residues before passing them to `CALVADOS_frontend`. If you need protein–RNA interaction analysis, use `Mpipi_frontend` exclusively.

Sources: [mpipi_frontend.py](finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L50-L75), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L17-L29)

## Method Override Summary

While the base class provides full implementations, each derived class overrides specific methods to inject model-specific behavior. The table below shows exactly which methods are overridden and why:

| Method | Overridden in Mpipi? | Overridden in CALVADOS? | Reason for Override |
|---|---|---|---|
| `__init__` | ✅ | ✅ | Bind different forcefield model and `IMC_object` |
| `intermolecular_idr_matrix` | ✅ | ✅ | Mpipi: auto-detect `U` → disable disorder; CALVADOS: `@RNA_check` decorator |
| `epsilon` | ❌ | ✅ | CALVADOS: `@RNA_check` decorator |
| `epsilon_vectors` | ❌ | ❌ | No model-specific validation needed |
| `interaction_figure` | ✅ | ✅ | Mpipi: auto-detect `U` → disable disorder; CALVADOS: `@RNA_check` + different `vmin`/`vmax` defaults |
| `per_residue_attractive_vector` | ❌ | ❌ | Inherited as-is |
| `per_residue_repulsive_vector` | ❌ | ❌ | Inherited as-is |
| `protein_nucleic_vector` | ❌ | ✅ (stub) | CALVADOS: raises exception — RNA unsupported |
| `build_phase_diagram` | ❌ | ❌ | Inherited as-is |
| `plot_phase_diagram` | ❌ | ❌ | Inherited as-is |
| `plot_multiple_phase_diagrams` | ❌ | ❌ | Inherited as-is |

Sources: [mpipi_frontend.py](finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L1-L292), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L1-L350)

## Choosing a Frontend

| Criterion | Use `Mpipi_frontend` | Use `CALVADOS_frontend` |
|---|---|---|
| Protein–protein IDR interactions | ✅ | ✅ |
| Protein–RNA interactions | ✅ | ❌ |
| Dielectric-based electrostatic control | ✅ | ❌ |
| pH/temperature-dependent protonation | ❌ | ✅ |
| Mpipi_GGv1 parameter set | ✅ | ❌ |
| CALVADOS2 parameter set | ❌ | ✅ |

For most protein–protein studies, either frontend will produce valid results, but the numerical values will differ because they encode different coarse-grained forcefield parameterizations. For protein–nucleic acid work, `Mpipi_frontend` is the only option.

**Next steps**: To understand the forcefield parameters that each frontend binds, see [Mpipi Forcefield Parameters](11-mpipi-forcefield-parameters) and [CALVADOS Forcefield Parameters](12-calvados-forcefield-parameters). For the computation engine that both frontends delegate to, see [InteractionMatrixConstructor](8-interactionmatrixconstructor). For visualization details, see [Interaction Maps and Figures](6-interaction-maps-and-figures).


# Interaction Maps and Figures



Interaction maps (intermaps) are the primary visual output of FINCHES, providing a two-dimensional heatmap that reveals how every local region of one intrinsically disordered region (IDR) is predicted to interact with every local region of another. They are generated through the **`interaction_figure()`** method on either the `Mpipi_frontend` or `CALVADOS_frontend` object, which internally computes a sliding-window epsilon matrix, overlays per-sequence disorder profiles, masks folded regions, and renders a publication-ready matplotlib figure in a single call.

## How Intermaps Work

An intermap is constructed by decomposing two sequences into overlapping fragments of `window_size` residues, then computing the pairwise epsilon (interaction energy) between every fragment from sequence 1 and every fragment from sequence 2. The resulting 2D matrix is displayed as a heatmap where the **x-axis** maps positions in sequence 1, the **y-axis** maps positions in sequence 2, and **pixel color** encodes the predicted interaction strength — negative (attractive) values in green and positive (repulsive) values in purple by default. Parallel bar tracks along the top and right edges show the predicted disorder probability for each residue, and folded domains are automatically zeroed out.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Two amino acid<br/>sequences &#40;seq1, seq2&#41;"] --> B["Sliding-window<br/>fragmentation<br/>&#40;window_size=31&#41;"]
    B --> C["Pairwise epsilon<br/>computation<br/>&#40;IMC_object&#41;"]
    C --> D["Raw interaction<br/>matrix &#40;2D ndarray&#41;"]
    D --> E{"null_shuffle<br/>enabled?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Subtract shuffled<br/>baseline matrix"]
    E -- No --> G["Proceed"]
    F --> G
    G --> H{"zero_folded<br/>enabled?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["Mask folded-domain<br/>regions to zero"]
    H -- No --> J["Proceed"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["Render heatmap +<br/>disorder bar tracks<br/>+ colorbar"]
    K --> L["Return fig, im,<br/>ax_main, ax_top,<br/>ax_right, ax_colorbar"]
```

The pipeline above shows the full decision flow from raw sequences through to the rendered figure. Each stage is configurable through the `interaction_figure()` parameter set.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L247-L399), [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L131-L198)

## Generating an Interaction Figure

The simplest usage requires only two sequences and a frontend object:

```python
from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import Mpipi_frontend

mf = Mpipi_frontend()

s1 = 'MESNQSNNGGSGNAALNRGGRYVPPHLRGGDGGAAAAASAGGDDRRGGAGGGGYRRGGGNSGGGGGGGYDRGYNDNRDDRDNRGGSGGYGRDRNYEDRGYNGGGGGGGNRGYNNNRGGGGGGYNRQDRGDGGSSNFSRGGYNNRDEGSDNRGSGRSYNNDRRDNGGD'
s2 = 'LEGMSGDMRSGGGYRGRGGRGNGQRFGGRDHRYQGGSGNGGGGNGGGGGFGGGGQRSGGGGGFQSGGGGGRQQQQQQRAQPQQDWWS'

# Generate the interaction figure (homotypic)
mf.interaction_figure(s1, s1, tic_frequency=15)

# Generate the interaction figure (heterotypic)
mf.interaction_figure(s1, s2, tic_frequency=15)
```

The method returns a tuple of matplotlib objects for further customization: `(fig, im, ax_main, ax_top, ax_right, ax_colorbar)`. If `no_disorder=True`, the return simplifies to `(fig, im, ax_main)`.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L247-L399), [interaction_matrix_demo.ipynb](demo/protein_matrix/interaction_matrix_demo.ipynb#L87-L120)

## Interaction Figure Parameters

The `interaction_figure()` method exposes extensive control over computation, visual styling, and domain annotation:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `seq1`, `seq2` | str | — | Amino acid sequences to compare |
| `window_size` | int | 31 | Sliding window length (must be odd) |
| `use_cython` | bool | True | Use Cython-accelerated matrix computation |
| `use_aliphatic_weighting` | bool | True | Weight aliphatic residues by local aliphatic density |
| `use_charge_weighting` | bool | True | Weight charged residues by local charge density |
| `tic_frequency` | int | 100 | Spacing between axis tick marks |
| `vmin`, `vmax` | float | -3, 3 | Color scale bounds (kT units) |
| `cmap` | str | `'PRGn'` | Matplotlib colormap name |
| `zero_folded` | bool | True | Set folded-domain pixels to zero |
| `disorder_1`, `disorder_2` | bool | True | Compute and display disorder profiles |
| `no_disorder` | bool | False | Omit disorder tracks entirely |
| `null_shuffle` | bool/int | False | Number of sequence shuffles for null baseline subtraction |
| `fname` | str | None | File path to save figure (None = display only) |
| `seq1_domains`, `seq2_domains` | list | [] | Domain regions to highlight as dark bars |
| `seq1_lines`, `seq2_lines` | list | [] | Vertical/horizontal reference lines |
| `plot_rectangles` | list | None | Custom rectangle overlays `[s1_start, s1_end, s2_start, s2_end, kwargs]` |
| `linewidth` | float | 1 | Width of domain-boundary lines |

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L247-L399)

## Figure Layout and Axes

The interaction figure uses `plt.subplot2grid((4, 4), ...)` to arrange four panels in a single figure:

| Axis | Grid Position | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `ax_main` | (1,0) colspan=3, rowspan=3 | 2D interaction heatmap |
| `ax_top` | (0,0) colspan=3 | Disorder bar plot for sequence 1 (vertical bars, 0–1 scale) |
| `ax_right` | (1,3) rowspan=3 | Disorder bar plot for sequence 2 (horizontal bars, 0–1 scale) |
| `ax_colorbar` | (0,3) | Color scale legend for the heatmap |

Domain highlights passed via `seq1_domains` or `seq2_domains` render as dark vertical or horizontal spans on the corresponding disorder track. Custom rectangles from `plot_rectangles` draw directly on `ax_main` as edge-only patches, useful for annotating specific interaction hot-spots.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L400-L560)

## Accessing the Raw Matrix

When you need the underlying numerical data for custom analysis or visualization, call `intermolecular_idr_matrix()` instead of `interaction_figure()`:

```python
# Returns (B, disorder_1, disorder_2)
result = mf.intermolecular_idr_matrix(s1, s2, window_size=31)

# Unpack the matrix tuple
B       = result[0]   # The interaction matrix structure
d1      = result[1]   # Disorder profile for sequence 1
d2      = result[2]   # Disorder profile for sequence 2

# B is itself a 3-element tuple:
matrix  = B[0]   # 2D numpy array of sliding epsilon values
idx_s1  = B[1]   # Index array mapping matrix columns to sequence 1 positions
idx_s2  = B[2]   # Index array mapping matrix rows to sequence 2 positions
```

The index arrays are necessary because the sliding window does not pad the sequences — the matrix edges start and end at positions that depend on `window_size`. Specifically, the first valid index is at `window_size // 2 + 1` and the last is at `len(seq) - window_size // 2`.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L58-L198)

## Null Shuffle Normalization

Setting `null_shuffle` to an integer (recommended: 100) subtracts a sequence-shuffled baseline from the interaction matrix. For each shuffle iteration, both sequences are randomly permuted, a new matrix is computed, and the mean across all shuffles becomes the null baseline. For **homotypic** interactions (seq1 == seq2), the null is symmetrized to avoid artifacts. This normalization highlights interaction patterns that depend on residue order rather than composition alone.

```python
# Normalize against 100 shuffled controls
mf.interaction_figure(s1, s2, null_shuffle=100, tic_frequency=15)
```

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L147-L192)

## Folded Domain Masking

When `zero_folded=True` (the default), the `interaction_figure()` method uses **metapredict** to identify folded domain boundaries and sets all matrix pixels corresponding to folded residues to zero. This prevents stably folded regions from contributing misleading interaction signals, since the coarse-grained forcefield models are calibrated for disordered contexts. The same folded boundaries are shaded in grey on disorder tracks when using `plot_protein_nucleic_vector()`.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L400-L440)

## Sequence Logo Visualizations (interlogo)

The `interlogo` module provides HTML-rendered sequence logos that color and size each residue according to its chemical context and interaction contribution. These are designed for Jupyter notebook display.

### Chemical Context Color Scheme

Residues are colored by chemical class using a fixed palette defined in `AA_COLOR`:

| Chemical Class | Residues | Color |
|---|---|---|
| Aromatic | Y, W, F | `#ff9d00` (orange) |
| Aliphatic | A, L, M, I, V | `#171616` (black) |
| Polar | Q, N, S, T, H, G | `#04700d` (green) |
| Negative | E, D | `#ff0d0d` (red) |
| Positive | R, K | `#2900f5` (blue) |
| Cysteine | C | `#ffe70d` (yellow) |
| Proline | P | `#cf30b7` (magenta) |

A separate `AA_CHARGE_COLOR` dictionary provides a charge-only view where only E/D (red) and R/K (blue) are colored; all others are black.

### Attractive and Repulsive Logos

```python
from finches.frontend.interlogo import plot_attractive_logo, plot_repulsive_logo

# Attractive logo: residues sized by favorable interaction contribution
plot_attractive_logo(s1, s2, mf, window_size=31, quantile_threshold=0.7)

# Repulsive logo: residues sized by unfavorable interaction contribution
plot_repulsive_logo(s1, s2, mf, window_size=31, quantile_threshold=0.7)
```

The `quantile_threshold` parameter (default 0.7) controls the visibility cutoff: residues below the threshold quantile of the size distribution are rendered in light grey (`#cccccc`) rather than their chemical class color, ensuring only the most interaction-relevant positions are visually prominent.

### Custom Chemical Context Plots

For manual control, `chemical_context_seq_plot()` accepts any sequence and a scaling vector:

```python
from finches.frontend.interlogo import chemical_context_seq_plot
import numpy as np

scale_vector = np.random.rand(len(s1))  # any per-residue values
chemical_context_seq_plot(s1, scale_vector, min_font_sz=8, max_font_sz=30, quantile_threshold=0.7)
```

Sources: [interlogo.py](finches/frontend/interlogo.py#L1-L270)

## Window Size Considerations

The default `window_size=31` was chosen empirically: ~30-residue IDRs represent a length scale where chemical specificity can be meaningfully encoded. Smaller windows increase spatial resolution but reduce the fragment length over which interaction energies are averaged, potentially introducing noise. Larger windows smooth over local variation but may miss fine-grained interaction patterns. When using non-default windows, adjust `vmin`/`vmax` accordingly since the energy range shifts:

```python
# Smaller window — narrower energy range
mf.interaction_figure(s1, s2, window_size=13, vmin=-2, vmax=2, tic_frequency=15)
```

Sources: [idr_idr.rst](docs/idr_idr.rst#L52-L67)

## Frontend Model Differences

Both `Mpipi_frontend` and `CALVADOS_frontend` expose the same `interaction_figure()` interface, but differ in their underlying forcefield and initialization parameters:

| Feature | Mpipi_frontend | CALVADOS_frontend |
|---|---|---|
| Forcefield | Mpipi_GGv1 | CALVADOS2 |
| Init params | `salt`, `dielectric` | `salt`, `pH`, `temp` |
| RNA support | Yes (via `U` in sequence) | No (raises `ValueError`) |
| Default salt | 0.150 M | 0.150 M |

The CALVADOS frontend applies an `@RNA_check` decorator that raises a `ValueError` if `'U'` appears in either input sequence, whereas the Mpipi frontend supports protein–nucleic acid interactions natively.

Sources: [mpipi_frontend.py](finches/frontend/mpipi_frontend.py#L1-L100), [calvados_frontend.py](finches/frontend/calvados_frontend.py#L1-L150)

> [!TIP]
> When generating interaction figures for publication, set `fname` to save at 350 DPI and manually adjust `tic_frequency` based on sequence length — use ~15 for sequences under 200 residues and ~100 for sequences over 500 residues to keep tick labels readable.

> [!TIP]
> The `plot_rectangles` parameter is the most flexible way to annotate interaction hot-spots: pass `[[s1_start, s1_end, s2_start, s2_end, {'edgecolor':'red', 'linestyle':'--'}]]` to draw styled rectangles directly on the heatmap without altering the underlying data.

# Per-Residue Interaction Vectors



Per-residue interaction vectors decompose a global ε interaction value into a **position-resolved profile**, revealing which residues in one sequence drive attractive or repulsive interactions with another sequence. This is the diagnostic lens that transforms a single scalar summary into a residue-by-residue map of interaction chemistry — essential for identifying "sticker" regions, understanding domain boundaries, and rationalizing mutational effects within intrinsically disordered regions.

## Conceptual Foundation

A per-residue interaction vector answers the question: *for each position i in sequence 1, what is the net interaction character with sequence 2?* The answer is not a single number but two complementary vectors — **attractive** and **repulsive** — each of length *N* (the number of residues in the reference sequence). These vectors are computed by collapsing the full sliding-window interaction matrix along one axis, applying sign-based masking to isolate attractive (ε < 0) from repulsive (ε > 0) contributions, and optionally smoothing the result.

This decomposition matters because averaging over a region can obscure the interplay of stickers and spacers: a region may be strongly attractive at a few positions yet repulsive elsewhere. Since repulsive regions in an IDR can reconfigure to avoid each other while attractive residues actively drive coalescence, the per-residue profile lets you identify putative sticker residues **without confounding by neighboring repulsive elements**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Sequences S1, S2"] --> B["Sliding-Window<br/>Interaction Matrix"]
    B --> C{"Sign-Based Masking"}
    C -->|ε < threshold| D["Attractive Mask"]
    C -->|ε > threshold| E["Repulsive Mask"]
    D --> F["Row-wise Summation<br/>(collapse S2 axis)"]
    E --> G["Row-wise Summation<br/>(collapse S2 axis)"]
    F --> H["Average or Total<br/>per residue"]
    G --> I["Average or Total<br/>per residue"]
    H --> J["Savitzky-Golay<br/>Smoothing"]
    I --> K["Savitzky-Golay<br/>Smoothing"]
    J --> L["(indices, attractive_vector)"]
    K --> M["(indices, repulsive_vector)"]
```

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L570-L696), [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L702-L828)

## Two API Layers: Frontend vs. Interaction Vector Module

Finches exposes per-residue interaction vectors through **two complementary API layers**, each suited to different workflows. The frontend layer provides the highest-level, most convenient access through methods on a `FinchesFrontend` object, while the `interaction_vector` module offers standalone functions with direct plotting capabilities.

| Feature | Frontend (`FinchesFrontend`) | Interaction Vector Module |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | `xf.per_residue_attractive_vector()` / `xf.per_residue_repulsive_vector()` | `show_sequence_interaction_vector()` / `show_folded_domain_interaction_vector()` |
| Returns | `(indices, values)` numpy arrays | matplotlib figure (or vectors if `return_vectors=True`) |
| Computation basis | Sliding-window matrix → row reduction | Direct `get_sequence_epsilon_vectors()` call |
| Smoothing | Built-in Savitzky-Golay | None (raw vectors plotted) |
| Folded domain support | No (IDR–IDR only) | Yes, via PDB surface residues |
| Logo visualization | Via `interlogo.plot_attractive_logo()` | Via `make_interaction_vector_plot()` |

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L570-L696), [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L100-L144)

## Frontend API: `per_residue_attractive_vector` and `per_residue_repulsive_vector`

These methods on any `FinchesFrontend` instance (e.g., `MpipiFrontend` or `CalvadosFrontend`) compute per-residue vectors from the full sliding-window interaction matrix. The computation proceeds in three stages: **matrix generation** → **masked row reduction** → **smoothing**.

### Attractive Vector

```python
from finches.frontend.mpipi_frontend import MpipiFrontend

xf = MpipiFrontend()

seq1 = "MDFFVLSVQEGDSNVQVDVLGATAAYSVLEA"
seq2 = "GSTDRRAGATQNEVSMVSQLQDKVKVLGAP"

indices, attractive_vals = xf.per_residue_attractive_vector(
    seq1, seq2,
    window_size=31,
    return_total=False,
    attractive_threshold=0,
    smoothing_window=20,
    poly_order=3
)
```

The function first calls `intermolecular_idr_matrix()` to obtain the sliding-window matrix *B*, then constructs an `attractive_mask` where `B < attractive_threshold`. Row-wise summation of `B * attractive_mask` yields the total attractive contribution per position. When `return_total=False` (default), this sum is divided by the count of attractive entries per row, giving the **average** attractive interaction; when `True`, the raw sum is returned, which can reveal regions with many modestly attractive residues that collectively drive binding.

> [!TIP]
> Setting `return_total=True` shifts the interpretation from "how attractive is each residue on average" to "how much total attractive pull does each residue experience" — the latter is more physically meaningful for predicting sticker-driven phase behavior, because multiple weak stickers can cooperate equivalently to fewer strong ones.

### Repulsive Vector

```python
indices, repulsive_vals = xf.per_residue_repulsive_vector(
    seq1, seq2,
    window_size=31,
    return_total=False,
    repulsive_threshold=0,
    smoothing_window=20,
    poly_order=3
)
```

The logic mirrors the attractive vector but applies `repulsive_mask = B > repulsive_threshold`. The same `return_total` flag controls average-vs-total behavior.

### Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `seq1` | str | — | First amino acid sequence (reference sequence for vector) |
| `seq2` | str | — | Second amino acid sequence |
| `window_size` | int | 31 | Sliding window size for interaction matrix |
| `use_cython` | bool | True | Use Cython-accelerated matrix computation |
| `use_aliphatic_weighting` | bool | True | Weight by local aliphatic residue density |
| `use_charge_weighting` | bool | True | Weight by local charge context |
| `return_total` | bool | False | Return sum instead of average per row |
| `attractive_threshold` / `repulsive_threshold` | float | 0 | Sign boundary for masking |
| `smoothing_window` | int / False | 20 | Savitzky-Golay window (False to disable) |
| `poly_order` | int / False | 3 | Savitzky-Golay polynomial order (False to disable) |

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L570-L696), [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L702-L828)

## Standalone Module API: `interaction_vector`

The `finches.interaction_vector` module provides four functions that operate independently of the frontend, offering both **IDR–IDR** and **IDR–folded domain** interaction vector computation with built-in matplotlib plotting.

### IDR–IDR Interaction Vectors

`show_sequence_interaction_vector()` computes and plots the per-residue interaction profile between two IDR sequences. It is a convenience wrapper over `epsilon_calculation.get_sequence_epsilon_vectors()` followed by `make_interaction_vector_plot()`:

```python
from finches.interaction_vector import show_sequence_interaction_vector
from finches.forcefields.mpipi import Mpipi_model
from finches.epsilon_calculation import InteractionMatrixConstructor

params = Mpipi_model(version='Mpipi_GGv1')
IMC = InteractionMatrixConstructor(parameters=params)

seq1 = "MDFFVLSVQEGDSNVQVDVLGATAAYSVLEA"
seq2 = "GSTDRRAGATQNEVSMVSQLQDKVKVLGAP"

fig = show_sequence_interaction_vector(
    seq1, seq2, IMC,
    charge_prefactor=None,
    null_interaction_baseline=None,
    use_charge_weighting=True,
    use_aliphatic_weighting=True,
    sequence_names=['Protein_A', 'Protein_B'],
    title=None
)
```

The returned figure displays the attractive vector (red) and repulsive vector (blue) as overlaid line plots, with residue positions on the x-axis. When `all_resi_labels=True` (default), x-axis tick labels show the actual amino acid residues **colored by their chemical class** (aromatic = orange, charged = red/blue, polar = green, aliphatic = black, cysteine = yellow, proline = purple).

### IDR–Folded Domain Interaction Vectors

`show_folded_domain_interaction_on_sequence()` extends interaction vector computation to the biologically critical case of an IDR interacting with **solvent-accessible residues on an adjoining folded domain**. It chains PDB structure parsing with interdomain vector computation:

```python
from finches.interaction_vector import show_folded_domain_interaction_on_sequence

fig = show_folded_domain_interaction_on_sequence(
    pdb='structure.pdb',
    FD_start=50,
    FD_end=150,
    sequence2='GGGGDDDDRRRR...',  # the IDR
    X=IMC,
    idr_position='Cterm',
    sequence_of_ref='sequence2',  # project onto the IDR
    sequence_names=['Full_protein', 'IDR_region']
)
```

The workflow first calls `pdb_to_SDFDresidues_and_xyzs()` to extract solvent-accessible folded domain (SAFD) residues and their 3D coordinates, then passes these to `get_interdomain_epsilon_vectors()` which accounts for **spatial proximity** — residues closer in 3D space to the IDR attachment point contribute more strongly. The `sequence_of_ref` parameter controls which sequence the vector is projected onto: `'sequence2'` (the IDR) or `'sequence1'` (the SAFD surface).

### Full Folded Domain Vector

`make_interaction_vector_for_folded_domain()` returns vectors of length equal to the **entire folded domain** (not just solvent-accessible residues). Buried positions are filled with zero, making the vector directly alignable with the full domain sequence:

```python
from finches.interaction_vector import make_interaction_vector_for_folded_domain

full_attractive, full_repulsive = make_interaction_vector_for_folded_domain(
    pdb='structure.pdb',
    FD_start=50, FD_end=150,
    sequence2='GGGGDDDDRRRR...',
    X=IMC,
    idr_position='Cterm'
)
# len(full_attractive) == FD_end - FD_start + 1
```

Sources: [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L19-L95), [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L100-L144), [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L256-L314)

## Visualization: Interaction Vector Plots and Sequence Logos

### Line Plot Rendering

`make_interaction_vector_plot()` renders the dual attractive/repulsive vectors as a matplotlib figure with configurable residue-labeled x-axis:

```python
from finches.interaction_vector import make_interaction_vector_plot

fig = make_interaction_vector_plot(
    attractive_vector, repulsive_vector, sequence1,
    sequence_names=['Protein_A', 'Protein_B'],
    title='Custom title',
    all_resi_labels=True,   # color-coded residue tick labels
    fig=None                # pass existing figure to overlay
)
```

The figure uses a dashed grey line at y=0 as the interaction baseline, with attractive values (negative, red) below and repulsive values (positive, blue) above. The figure width scales dynamically with sequence length at roughly `len(sequence) / 5.5` inches.

### HTML Sequence Logos

The `interlogo` module provides an alternative visualization that renders the amino acid sequence as an **HTML string with residue-specific font sizing**, where larger characters indicate stronger interaction. This is particularly effective in Jupyter notebooks for quick visual scanning of sticker positions:

```python
from finches.frontend.interlogo import plot_attractive_logo, plot_repulsive_logo

# Attractive logo: larger residues = more attractive
plot_attractive_logo(seq1, seq2, xf, window_size=31, quantile_threshold=0.7)

# Repulsive logo: larger residues = more repulsive
plot_repulsive_logo(seq1, seq2, xf, window_size=31, quantile_threshold=0.7)
```

The `quantile_threshold` parameter (default 0.7) controls a visual cutoff: residues below the 70th percentile of the interaction magnitude are rendered in light grey (`#cccccc`), drawing the eye to the strongest interactors. Residues are colored by chemical class using a 6-category scheme:

| Chemical Class | Residues | Color |
|---|---|---|
| Aromatic | Y, W, F | `#ff9d00` (orange) |
| Aliphatic | A, L, M, I, V | `#171616` (near-black) |
| Polar | Q, N, S, T, H, G | `#04700d` (green) |
| Negative | E, D | `#ff0d0d` (red) |
| Positive | R, K | `#2900f5` (blue) |
| Special | C, P | `#ffe70d` (yellow), `#cf30b7` (purple) |

The underlying `chemical_context_seq_plot()` function normalizes the interaction vector to a font size range (default 3–40 px) and delegates to `styled_text()` for HTML generation, inserting line breaks every 50 residues for readability.

Sources: [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L149-L253), [interlogo.py](finches/interlogo.py#L194-L268), [interlogo.py](finches/interlogo.py#L121-L173)

## Protein–Nucleic Acid Interaction Vectors

A specialized variant, `protein_nucleic_vector()`, computes per-residue interaction profiles between a protein and a poly-U RNA sequence. This sidesteps the full matrix construction and instead uses a **sliding-window epsilon calculation** against a fixed poly-U target:

```python
indices, binding_profile = xf.protein_nucleic_vector(
    seq='MDFFVLSVQEGDSNVQVDVLGATAAYSVLEA',
    fragsize=21,
    smoothing_window=30,
    poly_order=3
)
```

Each window of length `fragsize` in the protein is evaluated against a poly-U RNA fragment of the same length, and the resulting epsilon value (normalized by fragment length) is assigned to the window center. This produces a 1D profile of RNA-binding propensity along the protein chain.

Sources: [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L834-L872)

## Computation Pipeline Summary

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Interaction Vector Module"
        A1["show_sequence_interaction_vector()"] --> B1["get_sequence_epsilon_vectors()"]
        A2["show_folded_domain_interaction_on_sequence()"] --> B2["pdb_to_SDFDresidues_and_xyzs()"]
        B2 --> C2["get_interdomain_epsilon_vectors()"]
    end

    subgraph "Frontend Layer"
        D1["per_residue_attractive_vector()"] --> E1["intermolecular_idr_matrix()"]
        D2["per_residue_repulsive_vector()"] --> E2["intermolecular_idr_matrix()"]
        E1 --> F1["Mask + Row Sum + Savgol"]
        E2 --> F2["Mask + Row Sum + Savgol"]
    end

    subgraph "Visualization"
        G1["make_interaction_vector_plot()"]
        G2["plot_attractive_logo() / plot_repulsive_logo()"]
        G3["chemical_context_seq_plot()"]
    end

    B1 --> G1
    C2 --> G1
    F1 --> G2
    F2 --> G2
    G2 --> G3
```

Sources: [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L1-L16), [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L567-L696), [interlogo.py](finches/interlogo.py#L1-L48)

## Practical Considerations

**Smoothing is on by default.** The Savitzky-Golay filter (window=20, poly_order=3) removes high-frequency noise from the per-residue profile but can blur sharp transitions at domain boundaries. Disable it by passing `smoothing_window=False` or `poly_order=False` when you need the raw residue-level signal.

**Index offsets depend on window size.** Because the sliding-window matrix does not pad sequences, the returned index arrays start at `(window_size + 1) / 2` and end at `len(sequence) - (window_size - 1) / 2`. Always use the returned indices rather than assuming `range(len(sequence))`.

**The `sequence_of_ref` parameter matters for folded domains.** When computing IDR–folded domain vectors, `sequence_of_ref='sequence2'` projects the vector onto the IDR (useful for identifying which IDR residues are most influenced by the folded surface), while `sequence_of_ref='sequence1'` projects onto the SAFD surface (useful for mapping which surface patches interact most strongly with the IDR).

> [!TIP]
> For folded domain analysis, prefer `make_interaction_vector_for_folded_domain()` over `show_folded_domain_interaction_on_sequence()` when you need to align the vector with the full domain sequence (e.g., for overlay with other per-residue annotations), because the former returns vectors of the full domain length with zeros at buried positions.

Sources: [interaction_vector.py](finches/interaction_vector.py#L256-L314), [frontend_base.py](finches/frontend/frontend_base.py#L652-L696)
